newsitem.title: USA: Former Texaco executive expected to be indicted.
newsitem.headline: Former Texaco executive expected to be indicted.

text.p: Lawyers representing a former Texaco Inc. executive charged with destroying documents in a race discrimination case said on Friday that plea negotiations with prosecutors have ended.
The lawyers who represent Richard Lundwall said that talks collapsed after prosecutors refused to let them review a report written by an outside investigator for Texaco.

Lundwall was charged in November with obstruction of justice through a complaint filed by the Manhattan U.S. Attorney's Office. His lawyers said he is now expected to be indicted by a federal grand jury.
"They (prosecutors) said he would be indicted next week," said Christopher Riley, one of Lundwall's lawyers. Riley said negotiations would only resume at the request of federal prosecutors.
A spokesman for prosecutors said his office would not comment.
Ironically, the case against Lundwall stems from his own decision to come forward with evidence against himself and others in the discrimination case against Texaco.
In that class action suit, filed in 1994, a group of black employees alleged that Texaco discriminated against them in promotions and pay.

Lundwall, senior coordinator of personnel services for Texaco's finance department, had secretly taped conversations between himself and others in which they discussed destroying documents requested by the plaintiffs. When Lundwall was dismissed by Texaco in a downsizing move last summer, he gave the tapes to the plaintiffs lawyers.
After the tapes were made public in court proceedings, Texaco agreed to settle the case for $176.1 million. A fairness hearing on the settlement, which requires court approval, is set for March 18.
None of the some 1,300 potential plaintiffs in the case had opted out of the settlement as of the deadline earlier this week.
After the tapes were revealed, Texaco hired Michael Armstrong, a prominent Manhattan lawyer, to conduct an internal investigation.

After receiving the report in January, Texaco took action against executives heard on the tape, including Lundwall whose benefits were halted. The company also gave the report to prosecutors, who have kept it confidential.
Riley said that although Lundwall has cooperated with prosecutors they refuse to let him see Armstrong's report. He described the report as a "primary prosecutorial document."
"So, let him (Lundwall) have a public trial," Riley said. "He's cooperated with them and told him his story from start to finish ... enough is enough."
